$comment: The catalogues this repository generates. Read by `dcat` (--manifest) and by the
scheduled workflow in .github/workflows/nightly-catalogs.yml, so the list lives here
as data rather than being duplicated in CI configuration.
output paths are relative to this file.
version defaults to "latest", which resolves to the latest *stable* release.
language defaults to "cs".
The schema beside this file documents every key and is what an editor reads: a typo
is reported where it is typed, rather than by the tool after a package has been
downloaded.
This repository's own analyzers, catalogued by this repository's own generator. It reads a
project ALREADY BUILT rather than a NuGet package, because the analyzer it mirrors ships from
here: waiting for a published package would mean a new DCAT id could not be catalogued until
after it was released.
Consequence for any workflow running this manifest: DiagnosticCatalog.Analyzers must be built
first. Nothing here builds it. What that costs is now said by the tool rather than only here —
naming the path it looked at and the `dotnet build` that would produce it — so the reader who
meets it is the one who is told. Both callers build it today.
configuration is stated rather than left to its default, because it is what decides which
build is read and it used to be legible in the assembly path this entry replaced.
The NUnit analyzers. Not a transitive dependency the way xUnit's are — NUnit declares none
— but `dotnet new nunit` writes NUnit.Analyzers into the project file it generates, so a
test project has them without anybody having decided to.
The MSTest analyzers. Transitive, like xUnit's and unlike NUnit's: MSTest.TestFramework
depends on MSTest.Analyzers, so the MSTest meta-package and MSTest.TestAdapter both drag
them in. A test project has them without anybody choosing them.
The trimming, Native AOT and single-file warnings. The analyzer lives inside the SDK's own
Microsoft.NET.ILLink.Tasks package, which is public on nuget.org — so this entry is the
ordinary package shape despite the rules arriving through the SDK rather than a reference.
Blazor WebAssembly turns them on for every build without asking: its SDK props set
PublishTrimmed, and Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Analyzers.targets reads that to set EnableTrimAnalyzer.
The same holds for MAUI, for PublishAot, and for any library declaring IsTrimmable.
The ASP.NET Core and Blazor analyzers. Every Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web project runs them and
nobody installs them: they arrive inside the shared framework, and the web SDK references
that framework rather than any analyzer package.
Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Ref is the TARGETING PACK, and it is a perfectly ordinary package on
nuget.org — that is how the SDK acquires it. So this entry needs no special shape; reading
the pack from a feed is what makes the mirrored release one a consumer can also name.
The pack carries source generators beside the analyzers. They declare no rule of their own
here, so reading the whole pack yields exactly the rules the two analyzer assemblies do —
and naming the pack states what a consumer actually receives.
The .NET runtime's source-generator diagnostics. Microsoft.NETCore.App.Ref is the runtime
targeting pack, and like the ASP.NET Core one it is an ordinary package on nuget.org.
Six generator assemblies contribute: LibraryImport, the COM interface generator and its
shared source generation, the JavaScript JSImport generator, System.Text.Json's generator
and the regex generator. Only ten of their types declare a rule, and the whole pack is read
rather than a chosen subset so that a generator gaining its first rule is picked up by the
nightly instead of waiting for somebody to notice.
SYSLIB0xxx is absent on purpose: those are obsoletion warnings the compiler raises from
[Obsolete] on the API itself, not analyzer diagnostics, so no descriptor declares them.
The Roslyn analyzer-authoring rules. Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Analyzers reaches a project
TRANSITIVELY through Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp, so anyone writing an analyzer runs them
without having asked — the same shape as xUnit's and MSTest's.
Only THIS package is read. Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.PublicApiAnalyzers and
BannedApiAnalyzers carry the RS prefix too, and each has an entry of its own below: their
ids partition cleanly (RS00xx and RS0030/0031/0035 there, RS10xx and RS20xx here), and
reading several packages into ONE catalogue has no manifest shape anyway — `package` is a
single string, unlike `projects` and `assemblies`. What the three of them share is the
badge, and ADR-0035 decides it: the prefix stays with the catalogue already publishing it,
so this one keeps RS and the other two name their subject.
The public-API tracking rules. This is the first catalogue here that mirrors an analyzer
NOBODY RECEIVES BY ACCIDENT: Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.PublicApiAnalyzers is an explicit
PackageReference, chosen by a library that decided to track its surface in
PublicAPI.Shipped.txt and PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt. Every other entry in this file mirrors
an analyzer that arrives transitively or inside the SDK.
It earns its place on what happens after that choice rather than before it. RS0016 fires
once per member missing from the declared surface, so adopting the analyzer on an existing
library means meeting hundreds of them at once; the ones a team cannot resolve that day get
suppressed in source, which is exactly the position this library exists for.
SEPARATE from DiagnosticCatalog.Roslyn rather than merged into it. The ids do not collide
-- RS00xx here, RS10xx and RS20xx there -- and merging has no manifest shape anyway, since
`package` is a single string unlike `projects` and `assemblies`. The badge is what the two
of them do share: PackageIconTests asserts no two icons match, and ADR-0035 leaves RS with
DiagnosticCatalog.Roslyn and names this one after its subject, `API`.
The banned-API rules. Opt-in like PublicApiAnalyzers, and the smallest catalogue here: the
package declares three rules, one per symbol kind it can ban.
What it does is entirely driven by a BannedSymbols.txt the consumer writes, which is why the
rule count says nothing about how much a codebase sees. A team banning DateTime.Now or a
deprecated internal helper meets RS0030 on every remaining call site, and the ones that
cannot be migrated yet get suppressed in source with a justification.
Completes the RS family: RS00xx public-API tracking is DiagnosticCatalog.PublicApi, RS10xx
and RS20xx analyzer authoring is DiagnosticCatalog.Roslyn, and RS0030/0031/0035 are here.
Three catalogues rather than one because `package` is a single string; the badge each wears
follows ADR-0035 -- RS stays with the catalogue already publishing it, and the other two
name their subject: API, and BAN.
The xUnit.net analyzers. They reach a project TRANSITIVELY — xunit depends on
xunit.analyzers — so a test project has them without anybody choosing them, which is why
their rules are suppressed in source rather than configured away in .editorconfig.
The Roslyn IDE code-style rules. Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.CodeStyle is the package that
carries them; the same analyzers reach most projects through the .NET SDK instead, where
EnforceCodeStyleInBuild turns them on and .editorconfig sets their severity.
The package is versioned with the COMPILER, not with the SDK: installing one that declares a
newer compiler than the running one is refused with CS9057. That constrains which release a
consumer can install, and not what can be read here — dcat reads descriptors and runs no
analyzer — but it is why this catalogue rides a train of its own.
StyleCop.Analyzers' latest STABLE is 1.1.118, published in April 2019; the project has
lived on 1.2.0-beta ever since, and that is what projects actually install. Mirroring the
stable therefore mirrored a release almost nobody runs — and one rule already disagreed:
SA1413's category differs between the two, which nothing in a consumer's build would ever
report (§3.2). The rules live in StyleCop.Analyzers.Unstable; 1.2.0-beta of the main
package is a metapackage carrying no analyzer assembly. ADR-0016.
Every version of .Unstable is dash-free, so "latest" resolves within that line as usual.
